sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

candidates.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the \emph{bottleneck rank}, rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. candidates.title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset--receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. candidates.title: A Riemannian Geometry for Low-rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix $BA^\top$. This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation $(B, A) \sim (BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for any invertible matrix $G$ because $BA^\top = BG^{-1}(AG^\top)^\top$ and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices $(BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for all $G$ are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. In this paper, we propose a new Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. We theoretically show that LoRA with our preconditioning induced by this metric satisfies the following two properties at each

candidates.title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of $λ=0.01$ lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least $16$ relative to unpenalized LoRA. candidates.title: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $η_B / η_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $η_B$, the initialization scale $β$, and the adapter rank $r$. candidates.title: Normalize-Then-Precondition: A Hierarchical Approach to Marginal Scale and Interaction Geometry for LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix optimizers have emerged as a promising direction, with Muon standing out as a prominent design. Revisiting Muon through its full-Gram representation, we observe that it jointly processes marginal-scale and interaction information. This opens an alternative way to organize geometric information hierarchically, motivating the Normalize-Then-Precondition framework. Specifically, it first uses diagonal-Gram information to construct a marginally normalized update, then applies spectral preconditioning to its directional interaction geometry. Building on this framework, we develop NormPre with NormPre-G and NormPre-L adopting global and localized spectral preconditioning, grounded in spectral-norm steepest descent and a regularized formulation followed by leading mode selection, respectively. To enable large-scale training, NormPre-G uses Newton-Schulz iterations and NormPre-L employs randomized sketching to approximate the leading interaction eigenspace. Theoretically, we establish $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ convergence guarantees for simplified versions of NormPre. candidates.title: Rotated Manifold Optimization for Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

candidates.title: Beyond Low-Rank Parameterization: Narrowing the Gap Between LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning via Gradient Decomposition
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient. Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation). GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. candidates.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. candidates.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. candidates.title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. candidates.title: Robust Parameter-Efficient LLM Adaptation on Analog Hardware
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Analog in-memory computing is a promising platform for on-device execution of large language models because it performs matrix--vector multiplications (MVMs) in memory and in parallel, reducing data movement. However, limited digital-to-analog converter precision, input noise, and finite conductance states can degrade model accuracy, while full-model retraining to address these effects can be costly. We develop an optimizer-agnostic, parameter-efficient adaptation method based on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping the pretrained weights stored on analog arrays fixed while training the LoRA weights to adapt to downstream tasks and hardware non-idealities. Reliable adaptation requires handling errors in both forward and backward MVMs and physical weight updates. We use input reshaping to reduce input-induced MVM errors and update accumulation to retain small updates before programming them to finite-state analog devices. Across Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Llama-3-8B with both Muon and AdamW, input reshaping improves analog LoRA fine-tuning under noisy MVM computation. candidates.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. candidates.title: A Fine-Grained Analysis of the LoRA Fine-Tuning Landscape with Implications for Data Selection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. Existing theoretical analyses provide only limited guidance on this trade-off, and their guarantees are typically established under restrictive theoretical settings. We address this gap by developing a substantially sharper landscape theory for LoRA, building on modern results from nonconvex low-rank matrix sensing. candidates.title: FedLore: Communication and Memory Efficient Federated Learning via Shared Gradient Low-Rank Projection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters, but their fixed rank budget can limit adaptation. Thus, accurate local gradient compression need not preserve global descent. We propose \texttt{FedLore}, which shares a low-rank optimization basis within each round and refreshes it across rounds. The shared basis enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates and eliminates the identified projection bias. Subspace refresh allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. candidates.title: MLoRA:Continual Low-Rank Adaptation via Relative-Response Subspace Selection and Momentum Orthogonalization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) provides a parameter-efficient approach to continual learning, but its nominal rank can conceal a loss of effective adaptation capacity. We identify \emph{spectral plasticity collapse}: during sequential adaptation, update energy becomes concentrated in a small subset of singular modes, leaving much of the available low-rank space underutilized. This exposes a limitation of interference avoidance alone: protecting historical representations does not ensure that the remaining adaptation capacity is responsive to new tasks or effectively utilized. candidates.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. candidates.title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. These compact representations support both model updates and efficient policy synchronization. To prevent overly large updates from disrupting learning, we complement gradient compression with predicted-KL step control, which estimates policy changes before applying each update and adjusts its magnitude accordingly. With all techniques combined, LoGRA reduces average training memory usage by up to 45.7% across reasoning tasks without compromising performance. It also enables stable training of a 27B-parameter model for over 1,100 steps on a single eight-GPU node, where dense Adam runs out of memory, making previously memory-infeasible RL training practical. Code is available in the \href{https://github.com/skzhang1/labs-molt/tree/logra/examples/scripts/logra}{Molt library}.

candidates.title: From Spectra to Joint Schedules in LLM Pre-training: 3+3(+2) Scaling-Law Regimes
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Power-law learning curves are often treated as fixed properties of a model and its data, although learning-rate and batch-size schedules can change the observed loss. candidates.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. candidates.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. candidates.title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. candidates.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

candidates.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. candidates.title: Optimizer Geometry Sets the Pace: Spectral Learning Dynamics in Matrix Factorization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. candidates.title: Spectrally Targeted Muon
candidates.abstract_excerpt: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. candidates.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. candidates.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. candidates.title: LoRA's Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter's rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank.
